claims.text: The baseline consists of CoCrFeMnNi coatings on steel substrates with near-neutral residual stress.
Changing ion-beam energy and flux can systematically produce pronounced compressive versus near-neutral residual stress in CoCrFeMnNi coatings.
Increased compressive residual stress impedes microcrack initiation under mechanical loading.
Increased compressive residual stress impedes microcrack propagation under mechanical loading.
Residual stress generated during coating deposition can affect coating cracking.
Compressive residual stress modifies deformation behavior so that fewer microcracks accumulate during wear.
Accumulation and aggregation of wear-induced microcracks contribute to coating failure and material loss.
Coatings with higher compressive residual stress will have lower wear rates than near-neutral or tensile-stress coatings.
Coatings with higher compressive residual stress will have a lower density of microcracks than near-neutral or tensile-stress coatings.
The proposed effect should persist over a broad range of normal loads if deposition does not cause confounding microstructural changes.
Near-neutral-stress baseline coatings have higher microcracking and wear rates under otherwise identical conditions.
The mechanism holds within a moderate range of compressive stresses achievable by ion-beam assisted deposition.
Extreme residual stresses or dominant microstructural changes may limit the mechanism.
Grain size or phase distribution may covary with deposition-induced residual stress and confound its apparent relationship with wear.
Failure to observe a statistically significant reduction in both wear rate and microcrack density in the higher-compression group would falsify the hypothesis.
